findings.issue_text: [BUG] validates :email, email: true (app/models/user.rb:47) resolves the validator by constantizing the top-level constant EmailValidator, but the class is placed at lib/validators/email_validator.rb and the diff contains no autoload_paths change — with only lib on the autoload path, Rails maps lib/validators/email_validator.rb to Validators::EmailValidator, not EmailValidator, so the constant the model asks for is unresolvable. User class load raises ArgumentError 'Unknown validator: EmailValidator' at boot in lazily-loaded environments (and the new spec fails with NameError on describe EmailValidator), taking down the app, unless config.autoload_paths already listed lib/validators before this change — which no hunk in this diff establishes and no prior validator class in the visible context (username/password validation are model instance methods) would have required.

[ADVISORY] The blocked_emails feature ships with no writer anywhere in the diff: BlockedEmail records are created only by the new specs, and there is no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed path that inserts a row into the new table. BlockedEmail.should_block? can never return true in production, so the PR's headline validation is dead code on day one; site admins upgrading for this feature have no way to block an address except hand-writing SQL against the new table.

[ADVISORY] EmailValidator#validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?, which performs an unconditional SELECT plus a committed UPDATE (match_count increment, last_match_at stamp) as a side effect of running a validation. Every signup and email change pays an extra blocked_emails round-trip on a path that was previously pure in-memory validation, and because validations run before the user save transaction opens, the counter write autocommits even when the signup subsequently fails or valid? is called speculatively — permanently corrupting the match_count/last_match_at statistics those columns exist to record.

[ADVISORY] The client pushes the submitted address into rejectedEmails whenever result.errors.email is present, which includes uniqueness failures ('has already been taken'), and emailValid then renders the generic user.email.invalid format message for that address, discarding the server's specific reason string. A user whose email is already taken (or whose server-side block was since lifted) is told inline that the email format is invalid rather than the real problem, and because the create-account controller is a long-lived singleton the stale rejectedEmails entry keeps failing inline validation for that address for the rest of the session even after the underlying cause is resolved.

[ADVISORY] The new spec only exercises the BlockedEmail branch with should_block? stubbed out and never sets SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist or email_domains_blacklist, so the whitelist/blacklist branches and the errors-blank gating condition that were moved into EmailValidator have no coverage in this diff. A regression in domain restriction enforcement — the branch admins actually configure via site settings — or in the gating (e.g., should_block? silently skipped whenever any other email error is present) would ship unnoticed unless pre-existing user model specs happen to exercise the relocated logic.

[ADVISORY] BlockedEmail ships with no write path anywhere in the diff — no admin controller, route, API endpoint, rake task, or seed creates records — so the blocklist this entire feature validates against can never be populated outside the Rails console. Operators cannot block a single email address through the application, making the new table, the validator integration, and the client-side handling inert in production; the match_count/last_match_at statistics written by should_block? likewise have no reader anywhere (the spec comment at spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb:15-17 documents inspecting them only by manually loading the table), and the :do_nothing action exists solely for an admin surface that is not part of this change.

[ADVISORY] No test in the diff exercises the real integration: email_validator_spec stubs `BlockedEmail.stubs(:should_block?)` at lines 11 and 17, and blocked_email_spec tests the class method in isolation, so nothing verifies that creating a User whose email matches a real BlockedEmail record fails validation. A regression in the User→EmailValidator→BlockedEmail chain — e.g., the `record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` guard in lib/validators/email_validator.rb:15 short-circuiting incorrectly, or the blocked check never firing against real records — ships green, and the PR's core acceptance criterion (signup with a blocked email is rejected) is never demonstrated by any test.

[ADVISORY] The new failure-payload keys `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` are consumed by create_account_controller.js (`result.errors.email`, `result.values.email`), but no spec in the diff covers the controller's failure response — the diff adds only validator/model specs. A regression that renames or drops either key (or omits `values` when `errors` is populated) passes the entire test suite while silently disabling the client-side rejected-email memory; the server→client contract that the whole client feature depends on is unverified.

[ADVISORY] The client pushes `result.values.email` into rejectedEmails for ANY server email error — uniqueness ('has already been taken'), whitelist/blacklist ('not_allowed'), or blocked — not just blocked emails, and emailValid then renders the generic `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` for every such address. A user whose email was rejected as already taken sees the field flagged with a generic 'invalid' reason that contradicts the specific error shown in the flash message, and the state named rejectedEmails actually means 'any server-rejected email', so future changes to this path cannot assume it tracks blocked emails only.

[ADVISORY] The new behavior-bearing client logic — the rejectedEmails state (line 17), its population on failure (lines 274-276), and the `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` gate with the `rejectedEmails.@each` observer — has no test anywhere in the diff, which adds only Ruby specs. A regression in the client gating (the observer key, the contains check, or the push condition) silently breaks the only user-facing feedback for rejected emails, with no test in the diff to catch it.

[ADVISORY] Blocked-email matching is byte-exact: `BlockedEmail.where(email: email)` performs no case normalization, the BlockedEmail model normalizes nothing on write, and the client's `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` is case-sensitive, so nothing in the blocked-email path normalizes case on either side. A blocklist entry stored as 'Bad@Spammers.org' does not match a signup submitted as 'bad@spammers.org' (and vice versa), so blocking effectiveness depends on casing that nothing in the diff enforces — an obvious edge case no section of the change addresses.

[BUG] The diff ships the blocked_emails table (db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb) and the enforcement path, but contains no writer anywhere — no admin UI, controller action, rake task, or seed creates BlockedEmail records — so the blocklist can only be populated by direct database manipulation. The stated intent ('email validation for blocked users') is inert end-to-end: operators cannot block any email through any shipped interface, and the :do_nothing action type is unreachable; the feature only functions for someone with DB console access.

[BUG] The client pushes result.values.email into rejectedEmails on ANY server email error — including uniqueness ('has already been taken') and domain whitelist/blacklist failures, not just blocked-email rejections — and nothing in the diff ever removes entries from the list. Immediately after a routine 'email has already been taken' failure, the email field flips to the local 'invalid' message (contradicting the flash text), and that legitimate email stays locally unregistrable for the rest of the browser session even after the conflict is resolved, because the local check at lines 69-74 short-circuits before the server is consulted again.

[ADVISORY] should_block? writes match_count and last_match_at on every matching lookup, but no code in the diff ever reads these columns, and the write turns a validation-path predicate into a database mutation. Untraceable work: every signup attempt matching an entry performs a racy read-modify-write whose data nothing consumes, and any caller invoking user.valid? outside a save silently mutates the table; this telemetry is drift from the stated validation intent.

[ADVISORY] The :do_nothing action type has no producer and no consumer in the diff — nothing can create such a record, and its only behavior is skipping the block while still incrementing stats. Dead configuration surface that the spec enshrines (blocked_email_spec.rb exercises it) and future changes must preserve; a deletion opportunity unless a requirement names it.

[ADVISORY] The failure response of user creation now includes per-field errors and echoed name/username/email values for every failure mode, while the client consumes only errors.email and values.email, and no spec in the diff covers the new payload shape. The endpoint's response contract changes for all consumers (username taken, password too short, etc.) with nothing pinning the shape; a regression there silently breaks the client's rejectedEmails feedback loop.

[ADVISORY] Converting validates_presence_of :email / validates_uniqueness_of :email into the validates :email, presence/uniqueness form is behaviorally equivalent and not traceable to the blocked-email feature. Untraceable churn in a core model widens the review surface of a feature PR and invites conflicts with in-flight changes touching the same validation lines.

[ADVISORY] The local rejected-email check reports I18n.t('user.email.invalid') — the malformed-format message — instead of a 'not allowed' message, so the server's new user.email.blocked copy never surfaces on the client fast path. A user whose email is blocked is told their email address is invalid, sending them hunting for a typo that does not exist; the client half of the feature under-delivers the messaging the server half added.

[ADVISORY] Blocklist matching is exact case-sensitive string equality (BlockedEmail.where(email: email) against a case-sensitive unique index) with no case normalization anywhere in the diff, so an entry for 'spam@x.com' does not match a signup using 'SPAM@x.com'. The blocklist is trivially bypassed by varying letter case, and case variants occupy distinct rows under the unique index, undermining the feature's stated purpose — unless email downcasing exists upstream outside this diff, which nothing here establishes.

[ADVISORY] email_in_restriction_setting? matches the domain substring anywhere in the address (Regexp.new("@(#{domains})") is unanchored), so with a whitelist an address like user@allowed.com.evil.net passes because '@allowed.com' matches — behavior carried verbatim from the deleted User methods into the new shared validator. Whitelist restriction is bypassable with attacker-controlled subdomain addresses; republishing the logic in lib/validators entrenches it as the reusable implementation at exactly the moment the move made fixing it cheap.

[ADVISORY] The new EmailValidator spec stubs should_block? and exercises only the blocked-email branch; the whitelist and blacklist branches of the new validator have no coverage anywhere in the diff. A regression in the moved domain-restriction logic (regexp construction or branch polarity) would ship without a failing validator-level spec, silently disabling domain restrictions for every model that uses the validator.

[BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? increments match_count via a non-atomic read-modify-write (SELECT, then `record.match_count += 1` in Ruby, then `record.save`) with no atomic UPDATE, row lock, or optimistic-lock column. Two concurrent signup attempts matching the same blocked row both read the same match_count and the second save overwrites the first's increment, so match_count/last_match_at silently undercount block hits; the ignored `record.save` return value loses the update without any error even outside races — this needs `UPDATE ... SET match_count = match_count + 1` (or FOR UPDATE).

[ADVISORY] The diff adds the blocked_emails table, model, fabricator, and validator wiring but contains no writer anywhere — no admin controller, route, admin JS, rake task, or seed path creates BlockedEmail records. Operators cannot use the feature at all: blocked_emails ships empty, should_block? always returns false, and the entire blocking path is dead code until someone inserts rows directly into the database.

[ADVISORY] should_block? is a predicate with write side effects: it saves match_count/last_match_at (running BlockedEmail's full validation stack, including a uniqueness-validation SELECT) from inside email validation, and ignores the save's return value. Any future caller using should_block? as a pure check silently mutates stats, a failed stats save is dropped without error, and a retry storm against one blocked email serializes concurrent signups on that row's write lock during validation.

[ADVISORY] action_type is an integer discriminator with no CHECK constraint and no database default, so any out-of-range integer is storable and should_block? silently treats every value other than actions[:block] as do_nothing. A bad manual insert or future writer bug stores e.g. action_type = 2 and the email silently fails to block (fail-open) with no error, instead of the schema rejecting the illegal state.

[ADVISORY] The client pushes the email into rejectedEmails whenever result.errors.email is present for ANY reason — including 'has already been taken' from the email uniqueness validator — and emailValid (line 69) then reports it with the generic user.email.invalid message, so the new server-side user.email.blocked reason is never distinguished client-side. A user whose valid email is blocked or already registered is told their email is 'invalid'; with emailValid.failed gating submission they cannot resubmit to see the server's specific flash message and have no path to the real reason without reopening the modal.

[ADVISORY] The only spec for the new validator stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and invokes validate_each directly, so no test in the diff exercises the real integration: User's `validates :email, email: true` invoking this validator during a save, or should_block? running against a real blocked_emails row. A regression in the real path (the where(email:) lookup, the stats write, or how Rails invokes the validator on User) ships with a green suite; the first signal is production signups not being blocked.

[BUG] Nothing in this diff can create a BlockedEmail row — there is no admin UI, controller action, SiteSetting, rake task, or seed that writes to blocked_emails — so BlockedEmail.should_block? always queries an empty table and returns false, and no email is ever actually blocked. The PR's stated objective ('email validation for blocked users') is not delivered by the artifact: operators have no product surface to populate the blocklist, so the registration-blocking path never fires in production, and the match_count/last_match_at statistics and the :do_nothing action type have no reader or writer either — the objective silently shrank from 'block emails' to 'ship inert schema plus a validation hook' without an accepted decision to do so.

[BUG] The client pushes the attempted address into rejectedEmails on ANY email validation failure — including uniqueness ('has already been taken'), not just blocked-list rejections — and emailValid (lines 69-74) then reports that address as failed with the generic 'user.email.invalid' reason for the rest of the session, with no removal path. A registrant whose email failed for a reason that can disappear (the conflicting account is deleted, an admin relaxes the blacklist) is shown 'invalid' for that address until a full page reload, and the inline reason misreports the actual server error — the mechanism silently broadens the objective from 'blocked emails are invalid' to 'any email that failed once is invalid for this session'.

[BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? looks the address up with BlockedEmail.where(email: email) — an exact, case-sensitive match on PostgreSQL — and neither the validator nor the model normalizes case or whitespace before the lookup. Any case variant (BAD@SPAMCLUB.COM) or whitespace-padded variant of a blocked address passes the check and registers successfully, so the blocklist provides no real protection against the very addresses it lists.

[ADVISORY] EmailValidator#validate_each triggers BlockedEmail.should_block?, which performs a committed UPDATE (match_count += 1, last_match_at) as a side effect of model validation, so User#valid? now mutates the database. Every validation pass on a user whose changed email matches a blocked row writes to blocked_emails — including non-registration flows (user email change in preferences, admin edits, bare valid? calls) — inflating match_count with non-attempts; concurrent attempts race on the read-modify-write and lose increments; and every email validation pays an extra SELECT against blocked_emails even when the table is empty.

[ADVISORY] The only spec covering the blocked-email path stubs out BlockedEmail.should_block?, and no test in the diff exercises that a User with a blocked email actually fails validation, the relocated whitelist/blacklist branches, or the users_controller errors/values payload the client feature depends on. A wiring regression — the validator not being applied to User, the email_changed? condition changing, or the JSON payload shape drifting away from what create_account_controller.js expects — ships silently, because the PR's core behavior (a blocked email rejecting registration and surfacing in the UI) has zero end-to-end coverage.

[BUG] email_in_restriction_setting? builds the unanchored, case-insensitive regex @(#{domains}) from the whitelist setting and matches it anywhere in the email string, so attacker@allowed.com.evil.com satisfies a whitelist entry for allowed.com while its real mail domain (evil.com) is attacker-controlled. With email_domains_whitelist enabled, any attacker who owns any domain can add an MX record for <whitelisted-domain>.<their-domain> and register accounts from a domain the admin never allowed, defeating the allowlist entirely; the same unanchored match simultaneously rejects legitimate user@sub.allowed.com addresses, confirming the check is not domain-aware in either direction.

[ADVISORY] should_block? matches the submitted email by exact string equality (BlockedEmail.where(email: email), a case-sensitive comparison in PostgreSQL), so a blocked address is evaded by plus-tagging (user+anything@spam.com), Gmail dot-collapsing (u.s.e.r@gmail.com), or case variation unless the email is downcased upstream of validation. Admins who block an address get no protection against the same mailbox under trivially different spellings — the control fails for exactly the repeat-abuse case it exists for, and nothing signals to the admin that the block is porous.

[ADVISORY] The diff ships the blocked_emails table, model, and validator wiring with no writer anywhere in the change — no admin controller, route, serializer, rake task, or seed path creates BlockedEmail records (only the test fabricator does). Operators deploying this cannot populate the blocklist through any product surface; the feature silently does nothing unless someone inserts rows directly into the database, so the 'blocked users' validation advertised by the PR is unusable as shipped.

[ADVISORY] The new JSON contract fields errors: user.errors.to_hash and values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email") added to the failed-signup response have no test anywhere in the diff. A regression that drops or renames values/errors passes CI and silently breaks the client's rejected-email feedback loop (create_account_controller.js pushes result.values.email into rejectedEmails to drive the inline 'invalid' state), so blocked users lose the signup error signal with no failing test to catch it.

[ADVISORY] The new client-side behavior — the rejectedEmails branch (lines 69-74), the new 'rejectedEmails.@each' observer dependency (line 96), and the pushObject failure path (lines 274-276) — has no test anywhere in this diff; the only specs added (spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb, spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb, spec/fabricators/blocked_email_fabricator.rb) cover the Ruby side only. The user-facing half of the feature — showing 'invalid' feedback the moment a server-rejected email is re-entered — can silently no-op (observer not firing on pushObject, contains() mismatch, undefined pushed from result.values.email) while the suite stays fully green; every regression in this controller ships undetected.

[ADVISORY] The new failure-payload fields (errors: user.errors.to_hash, values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")) that the client reads as result.errors.email and result.values.email have no controller spec in this diff, so the server-writer/client-reader key agreement is pinned by no assertion. If the payload shape drifts (values nil, key renamed, errors shape changed), the client pushes undefined into rejectedEmails and contains() never matches — the rejection cache silently stops working and users can retry a blocked email indefinitely, with all tests green.

[ADVISORY] Both examples stub BlockedEmail.should_block?, so the new short-circuit gate in lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 (`if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`) is never triggered — no test exercises a record that already carries a domain whitelist/blacklist error, and the moved domain branches (email_validator.rb lines 4-12) have no direct test in this diff either. A regression in the gate — e.g., running the blocked check unconditionally and stacking a second error onto domain-rejected emails, or inverting the blank? check — passes the suite; the validator↔BlockedEmail seam is only ever verified as two halves (stubbed validator spec plus direct model spec) that never run together.

[ADVISORY] The example named 'returns false if a record with the email doesn't exist' verifies only falsiness: should_block? returns nil when no record matches (blocked_email.rb line 17, `record && record.action_type == actions[:block]`, short-circuits to nil), and RSpec's be_false passes for nil, so the assertion cannot distinguish the claimed false from nil. A refactor that flips the no-record return value between nil and false is invisible to the suite, and any caller that ever compares should_block?(email) == false breaks undetected.

[ADVISORY] The 'adds an error when email matches a blocked email' example asserts only `record.errors[:email].should be_present` and never checks the message, so the new user.email.blocked locale string added in this diff (config/locales/server.en.yml) is verified by no test. A regression that reports user.email.not_allowed instead of the blocked message — or a misspelled/missing user.email.blocked key that renders 'translation missing' to users — passes the suite, leaving the two rejection paths indistinguishable to tests.

[ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table has no writer anywhere in this diff — no admin UI, controller route, rake task, or seed creates BlockedEmail rows — so should_block? can never match a real email unless an operator inserts rows manually via console or SQL. The enforcement path and its statistics columns (match_count, last_match_at) are inert in production: admins have no way to add a blocked email or set the do_nothing action, so the PR's core feature cannot fire for any real address until the table is hand-populated.

[ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table ships with no writer anywhere in this diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed path creates BlockedEmail rows, and the only write path in the new code (BlockedEmail.should_block?) merely updates pre-existing rows — so the feature this PR exists for is inert on any deployed site. Operators cannot block a single email through the application; the table stays empty forever unless someone hand-writes INSERT statements (the spec comment 'If we manually load the table with some emails' confirms manual SQL is the expected workflow), and because action_type is NOT NULL with no DB default (line 5), such manual inserts fail outright unless the operator knows the undocumented integer value of actions[:block].

[ADVISORY] should_block? increments match_count with a non-atomic read-modify-write (record.match_count += 1 followed by record.save) instead of an atomic UPDATE match_count = match_count + 1, so concurrent validations matching the same blocked email lose increments. Under concurrent signup attempts against the same blocked address, match_count silently undercounts and last_match_at can be written from a stale read, so the match statistics this table exists to collect are unreliable; the data-integrity fix is a one-line atomic update_all, but as written the counter drifts whenever traffic is concurrent.

[BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? looks up with a case-sensitive exact WHERE clause (BlockedEmail.where(email: email) on a plain Postgres string column) and neither the model nor the lookup applies any downcasing, so a block entry only ever matches byte-identical email strings. Nothing in the model normalizes case on either side, and with no writer UI in this diff nothing enforces lowercase at entry time either.

Operators cannot actually block any email through the application: the new BlockedEmail model, the should_block? branch in EmailValidator, and the client-side rejectedEmails UX are all dead code until someone hand-inserts rows via rails console/SQL, so the PR's headline feature is unusable in production as shipped.

[BUG] The new rejected-email branch reports every server-side email rejection as I18n.t('user.email.invalid'), misdescribing blocked, domain-blacklisted, and already-taken emails as 'invalid'. After one failed attempt, the persistent inline validation (which feeds submitDisabled) tells the user their well-formed email is 'invalid', while the actual reason ('is not allowed.' / 'has already been taken') appears only in the transient flash — the user retypes a valid-format address or debugging focuses on email syntax instead of the blocklist, misrepresenting the behavior to the user.

[ADVISORY] should_block? increments match_count via a non-atomic read-modify-write (record.match_count += 1 then record.save, return value unchecked) and performs this UPDATE on every validation attempt of the email, including attempts that fail for unrelated reasons and records with action_type :do_nothing. Concurrent signup attempts against the same blocked address — exactly the spam scenario the feature targets — read the same count and write it back, losing increments, and a failed stats write vanishes with no log, so match_count/last_match_at (the admin's only signal that a block is being hit) silently drift from reality; a signup flood against one blocked address also serializes every attempt on that single row's UPDATE.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] EmailValidator#validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?, which performs an unconditional SELECT plus a committed UPDATE (match_count increment, last_match_at stamp) as a side effect of running a validation. Every signup and email change pays an extra blocked_emails round-trip on a path that was previously pure in-memory validation, and because validations run before the user save transaction opens, the counter write autocommits even when the signup subsequently fails or valid? is called speculatively — permanently corrupting the match_count/last_match_at statistics those columns exist to record.

[ADVISORY] The client pushes the submitted address into rejectedEmails whenever result.errors.email is present, which includes uniqueness failures ('has already been taken'), and emailValid then renders the generic user.email.invalid format message for that address, discarding the server's specific reason string. A user whose email is already taken (or whose server-side block was since lifted) is told inline that the email format is invalid rather than the real problem, and because the create-account controller is a long-lived singleton the stale rejectedEmails entry keeps failing inline validation for that address for the rest of the session even after the underlying cause is resolved.

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, any failed signup where `result.errors.email` is present causes the submitted email (`result.values.email`) to be pushed into `rejectedEmails` (lines added near `pushObject`). On subsequent inline validation, `emailValid` short-circuits when `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` and returns `failed: true` with the generic `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`, regardless of the server’s actual email error (e.g. uniqueness/"has already been taken", domain restrictions, blocked email). Since the array is never cleared, the same email will continue to fail inline validation for the lifetime of that controller instance, even if the underlying server-side reason changes. This misleading/sticky behavior is directly introduced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Blocklist matching is exact case-sensitive string equality (BlockedEmail.where(email: email) against a case-sensitive unique index) with no case normalization anywhere in the diff, so an entry for 'spam@x.com' does not match a signup using 'SPAM@x.com'. The blocklist is trivially bypassed by varying letter case, and case variants occupy distinct rows under the unique index, undermining the feature's stated purpose — unless email downcasing exists upstream outside this diff, which nothing here establishes.
matched_golden_ids: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue describe the same underlying problem: `BlockedEmail` performs a case-sensitive email comparison/lookup, allowing blocked emails to be bypassed by changing letter case (e.g., 'User@Example.com' vs 'user@example.com'), leading to ineffective blocking/unauthorized access.

Whitelist restriction is bypassable with attacker-controlled subdomain addresses; republishing the logic in lib/validators entrenches it as the reusable implementation at exactly the moment the move made fixing it cheap.
matched_golden_ids: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Yes. Both point out that the regex `@(#{domains})` in `email_in_restriction_setting?` is not properly anchored/boundaried, so it can match a whitelisted domain as a substring and allow bypass via attacker-controlled domains like `evil.example.com` or `allowed.com.evil.net`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? increments match_count via a non-atomic read-modify-write (SELECT, then `record.match_count += 1` in Ruby, then `record.save`) with no atomic UPDATE, row lock, or optimistic-lock column. Two concurrent signup attempts matching the same blocked row both read the same match_count and the second save overwrites the first's increment, so match_count/last_match_at silently undercount block hits; the ignored `record.save` return value loses the update without any error even outside races — this needs `UPDATE ... SET match_count = match_count + 1` (or FOR UPDATE).

adjudication.rationale: In the new `BlockedEmail.should_block?` method, it fetches a row (`where(...).first`), then does `record.match_count += 1` and `record.last_match_at = ...` followed by `record.save` (app/models/blocked_email.rb). This is a classic non-atomic read-modify-write; concurrent calls can overwrite each other’s increments and timestamps, undercounting `match_count` and potentially regressing `last_match_at`. Also, the return value of `record.save` is ignored, so a failed save would silently drop the stats update.

A bad manual insert or future writer bug stores e.g. action_type = 2 and the email silently fails to block (fail-open) with no error, instead of the schema rejecting the illegal state.

So an out-of-range value (e.g., from manual SQL or corrupted data) would indeed “fail open” and allow emails that might be intended to block. This is a real integrity/robustness concern grounded in the diff, but it’s not an immediate functional defect under normal app writes (which set defaults) unless bad data is introduced.
